title: the plate that tells a story
hook: a bone, an egg, parsley and horseradish: the Passover plate, and why the answer starts with we

segments.voice: Yesterday: mensch, a decent human being. Your line was be a mensch. Today, a plate where every food is part of a story.

A spring night, a long table, chairs borrowed from the neighbors. In the middle sits a plate with odd little things on it: a roasted bone, an egg, some parsley, horseradish, a brown sweet paste. Nobody's eating them yet. Then the youngest kid stands up, a little nervous, and asks: why is this night different from all other nights?
screen: `A BONE, AN EGG, PARSLEY.` → `THE YOUNGEST STANDS UP.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: Seder means order. Passover night follows a set order of steps, read from a little book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. The story it tells is the Exodus: slaves in Egypt, a stubborn king, ten plagues, and a night of leaving so rushed the bread had no time to rise. That's the matzah. The plate is the story laid out as food. Bitter herbs, often horseradish, for how bitter slavery was. Charoset, a sweet paste often made of apples, nuts and wine, looks like the mortar the slaves used for bricks. A green vegetable, often parsley, dipped in salt water, like tears. The roasted bone recalls the lamb of the first Passover; the egg, an offering brought on festivals long ago. You taste the story before anyone explains it. Then comes the surprise. The answer to the child's question doesn't start with once upon a time. It starts: we were slaves. We. The old rule is that in every generation, each person should see themselves as if they personally walked out of Egypt. Not a history lesson. A memory you're handed.
screen: `SEDER — ORDER.` · `THE BREAD THAT DIDN'T RISE.` · `THE STORY LAID OUT AS FOOD.` · `WE WERE SLAVES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: something bitter from this year. Second breath: something sweet that came anyway. Third breath: hold the two together, the bitter and the sweet, the way the plate does.
Seder. Order: Passover night told step by step, with the story laid out on a plate. Fourth word.
Your line: we were slaves. Not they. We. That one word carries the whole night. Day four.

howItsDone: On the first night of Passover (the first two, for many outside Israel), Jewish families hold a seder, reading the Haggadah around the table: the youngest asks the four questions, the story is told in the first person, and matzah, bitter herbs, charoset and a green vegetable in salt water are eaten as part of the telling.

story.title: the basket in the reeds
story.text: A king orders every newborn boy among the slaves thrown into the river. One mother hides her baby for three months, until she can't hide him any longer. She seals a basket with tar, lays him in it, and sets it among the reeds, while his older sister watches from a distance. The king's own daughter comes down to bathe, hears the baby crying, and takes pity on him. His sister steps forward, offers to find a nurse, and runs to bring back his mother. The princess names him Moses.

Old day 11 (the Exodus) moved to day 4 and rebuilt around the seder plate (research: 'the seder plate'); the word changed from the Exodus to seder, so the strand teaches the object people actually sat in front of. Plate symbolism (maror, charoset as mortar, karpas in salt water as tears, zeroa for the Passover lamb, beitzah for the festival offering) is the common explanation; customs differ (romaine or horseradish for maror; parsley, celery or potato for karpas; Sephardi charoset often uses dates).
